reply.text: Qd5 develops the queen with an eye on c5 and f7, but the engine rates it a mistake (-1.34). Black answers with ...Qe7, defending the bishop and keeping the extra pawn. The queen then has to run again, while Black develops with tempo. Gambit play needs quick development, and here the queen costs you time. Want to try another move?

judge.note: The reply points at the development-with-tempo idea without naming Bxf7, but it pads with about six separate points and names the motif outright, which the attempt rung should avoid.

reply.text: Look at Black's king. Which Black pieces are defending the squares around it, and what happens to that cover if one of them is removed? Ask what a forcing first move could open up before you spend time developing.

judge.note: The nudge points at Black's king cover and a forcing first move without naming Bxf7+ or any square, which fits the nudge rung and a 1655 player's level.

reply.text:
Focus on f7. It's defended only by the king, and your bishop on c4 already hits it. Ask what happens if that pawn is taken with check and the king has to recapture. Which of your pieces could then arrive with check, and which Black piece would it attack?

See if the queen can hit c5 with tempo after the king is dragged forward.

judge.note: The reply names the f7 pressure and deflection idea without stating the move, but it points at the Bxf7+ sacrifice too directly (highlighting f7, c4, and the queen to c5 with tempo), which is close to a near-best candidate and arguably gives it away at the hint rung.

reply.text:
The best move is Bxf7+. After Kxf7, Qd5+ comes with check and the queen then takes the bishop on c5. The engine gives +0.67 for this line.

- The idea: sacrifice the bishop to drag the king out and win the c5 bishop, so you win material back at once.
- It also fixes what Qd5 did wrong. There the queen came out early and Black kept the extra pawn with ...Qe7.
reply.motif: desperado sacrifice / double attack with check

judge.note: At the move rung it names Bxf7+ and conveys the desperado sacrifice idea of dragging the king out and winning back the c5 bishop with a check-based double attack, with a short line and no jargon beyond what fits a 1655 player.

reply.text:
Bxf7+ works because the king has to come forward and Black's bishop on c5 is loose.

- The line: Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ Kf8 Qxc5+ d6 Qxc3 Qf6 O-O Ke8 Be3 Qxc3 Nxc3. You win the bishop back, regain the c3 pawn and Black's king stays uncastled. The engine gives +0.67.
- Qd5 went for the same two targets, but without check. Black answered ...Qe7, kept the extra pawn and developed with tempo. That left you at -1.34.
- O-O and Qb3 are the other candidates. Both keep the gambit going with development, but they only get about equality.
reply.motif: deflection / overloaded defender (sacrifice to win loose bishop)

judge.note: Explain rung names the sacrifice idea and the loose c5 bishop, gives the full line and why Qd5 allowed ...Qe7, and fits a 1655 player's level with a named tactic and short line, though it runs slightly past three points and the 'works because' opener is fine.

reply.text:
Nh4 attacks the queen, so it looks forcing. But the queen has a good reply. Qh5 pins the b5 queen against nothing, yet it offers a queen trade on the engine's terms: after Be2 a6 the white queen on b5 gets hit, and the line ends with White down material (eval -0.69). It also leaves the pawn on c3 alone, and Black's extra pawn keeps cramping you.

Think about what your pieces are owed here, and what the opponent's c3 pawn is doing. Want to try another move?

judge.note: The reply points at the c3 pawn and piece development without naming Nxc3, though the c3 pointer sits close to the best move and the Qh5 and Be2 lines are muddled.

reply.text: Look at the pawn on c3. It's the reason Black is ahead in material, and it also points at your king's side of the board. Ask yourself: is there a way to win it back with a developing move, while your queen is still safe on b5? Check what your minor pieces can still do before you start chasing the queen.

judge.note: Points at the c3 pawn and the material/recapture idea with a developing-move hint, without naming Nxc3 or any square, which suits the nudge rung and a 1664 player.

reply.text: Your knight on b1 is the piece doing nothing. The black pawn on c3 is the target, and it's attacked once the right piece comes in. Taking it also keeps your queen on b5 and your bishops pointed at f7 and the black king's side. Which piece can win it back while developing?

reply.text: The move is Nxc3. It wins the pawn back and develops the knight that has done nothing so far. It also keeps your queen on b5 and your bishops aimed at f7 and the black king, so you keep the initiative. The engine gives it +1.86, while Nh4 drops to -0.69.

judge.note: The move rung correctly names Nxc3 and the idea of recapturing with development while keeping the initiative, with depth suitable for a 1664 player, though it adds a few eval numbers and a fourth point that slightly pads the reply.

reply.text:
Nxc3 recaptures the pawn and brings the last piece into play, while Bc4 and Bg5 keep pressing on f7 and the black king.

- Nh4 chases the queen, but Qh5 answers it. After Be2 a6 your queen is hit, and the engine's line ends with you worse at -0.69. You spent a tempo and left c3 where it was.
- The engine's main line: Nxc3 a6 Qb3 Nge7 Rad1 Bg4 Nd5. Your pieces gain tempo with each move, and Black's king stays uncomfortable.
- Bd5 is also strong at +1.44. It shares the idea of rapid development with pressure on f7.

judge.note: Explain rung correctly gives the line and motif, but it pads with a third bullet and opens with a restated move, and phrases like 'You spent a tempo' and the mismatch between Nh4 and Qh5 concern lean toward judgmental framing; the depth suits a 1664 player.

reply.text:
2...e5 is a gambit-style break, but it's a mistake here. After dxe5 Black has no clear follow-up, and the engine's line has White keeping the extra pawn with a comfortable position (about -1.6 for you).

- It strikes the center before your pieces are ready.
- The d4 pawn can simply take, and your knight gets pushed around trying to regain it.

Try another move that fights for the center while keeping the structure sound.

reply.text: Ask yourself: which of your pawns can challenge d4 without giving White a free capture? Look for a setup where every pawn move is supported by a piece or by another pawn, so your center and development stay in step.
